whatItIs.text: Ground, dry-roasted peanuts — usually with salt, sometimes sugar or emulsifiers; the most common of the nut butters and protein-rich for a spread.

historyNote.text: Aztecs and Incas ground roasted peanuts into paste centuries ago; the modern version began with a Montreal patent in 1884, was served to patients at John Harvey Kellogg's sanitarium, and started life as a food for the wealthy. George Washington Carver famously did not invent it.

howToChoose.text: Check the label: natural styles list peanuts (and salt) only and need stirring; conventional no-stir jars use emulsifiers. Crunchy or smooth is a household referendum.

storage.text: Natural jars keep in the fridge to slow oil separation; stir and reseal. The rulebook has the details.

foodSafetyRef.note: opened-jar guidance lives in the food-safety rulebook

useItUp.text: Peanut butter rescues more than toast: whirl into satay sauce, blend into smoothies or banana nice-cream, or bake into cookies when the sweet tooth strikes.

substitutions.note: gentler flavour, similar fat; usually pricier
